== 
'''TAMARA ADIRA''' ==

<gallery>
Known for: Performance art, flamenco
Notable works: SONIDOS DE LIBERTAD, MERCURIA, ESTRELLAS
Awards:  Grants, Texas Commission of the Arts, San Antonio Department of Arts and Culture, Artist Foundation
</gallery> 

'''Tamara Adira''' (Born 1969) is an American performance artist, dancer, director, and writer who lives and works in Spain and Texas. Adira has taken a variety of approaches to her art, including installations, performance art, dance, music, and storytelling. Her work is heavily influenced by flamenco and is infused with human rights activism. 

'''Early Work and Background'''
Tamara Adira (nee Tamara Schulman) was born in Richmond, Virginia of Ashkenazi and Sephardic Jewish descent to a family who placed a large focus on the arts in a strict traditional culturally Jewish upbringing, studying ballet, music and art classes from age 4 through to college. She went to Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the Harvard Graduate School of Design, and later Tulane University. 
At MIT, she studied architecture and visual arts, working in the Media Lab and the Center for Advanced Visual Studies, where she created a project exploring the integration of electronic components into costume. Her project, selected to appear at the Boston First Night parade, was awarded recognition under the MIT Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program for early innovation in technology. Tamara Adira was given opportunities to work and study in the Avant Garde movement and did a residency and performance at Harvard in 1989 under John Cage with a theatrical solo combining performance art, movement, and voice.<sup>https://voyagesanantonio.com/interview/community-highlights-meet-tamara-adira-of-arte-y-pasion/ </sup>

At Tulane University, she first started studying flamenco in 2000. In 2010, she founded Arte y Pasión, which would later become the 501c3 nonprofit, the Arte y Pasion Flamenco and Spanish Dance Company. Adira studied with such artists as Teo Morca, Belén Maya, Daniel Caballero, Nino de los Reyes, Jose Maya, Belén Lopez, Oruco, and Andrés Marin. 


'''Arts Activism and Storytelling'''
Throughout her career, Adira has shined a light on human rights issues, taking a storytelling approach to her work to speak out on specific subject matter. In 2025, Adira produced and directed SONIDOS DE LIBERTAD  “Sounds of Liberty,” a history of Punk and its origins speaking out against authoritarianism in the United States, as told through the language of flamenco. In 2024, Adira produced and co-directed MINHA , a prayer calling for peace in Gaza. In 2023, Arte y Pasión produced and directed MERCURIA, an anthem to the impossible choices women must make in pursuit of their own agency.  MINHA was co-directed, and MERCURIA  was directed under the mentorship of Belén Maya , . In 2020, MANTAS DE LUZ illuminated the inhumane confinement of migrants.  From 2016-18, Adira produced and directed ESTRELLAS,  both a dedication to the ancestors of American Holocaust survivors and a warning that the same thing might happen in the United States if xenophobic immigration policies remained unchecked. In 2016, COLORES  celebrated the story of human diversity, showcasing the distinctions between us through our emotions, temperaments and symbology.  In 2014-15, ANGEL OF GRAVITY  told the story of the immense destruction caused by narcissism and the path towards healing . 

Outreach
Since 2010, Adira has led cultural exchange projects and programming expanding public access to flamenco through intercultural exchange with artists from Spain, community performances, and workshops through Arte y Pasión. In 2023 Adira spearheaded a campaign through Arte y Pasión in partnership with San Antonio We Flamenco Fest and Heritage Festivals, that resulted in the City of San Antonio designating November 16 2023 as “International Day of Flamenco,”  continuing the citywide observance through 2024 and 2025.  Throughout her career, Adira’s nonprofit efforts have promoted free public events, arts education, multicultural exchange, and outreach to schools, shelters, and clinical care facilities across underserved communities in Texas.   

Expansion
In November 2025, Adira expanded efforts across the Atlantic, still maintaining a performance and outreach presence in Texas, but also performing and producing in Europe and the Middle East. The company was recently recognized in Fullbright Scholar Dr. Claudia Green’s publication “Flamenco for the Future: A Stakeholder Approach to Cultural Sustainability,” presented at the International Conference for Tourism and Biodiversity at Marrakech, Morrocco and debuted tablaos in Sevilla, Spain fostering intercultural exchange between artists from Spain, France, the US, and the Middle East .

== Plot ==
In 1944, at the height of the Second World War, the [[Allies of World War II|Allied powers]] prepare to invade [[German-occupied Europe]] under [[Operation Overlord]]. Helmed by Gen. [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] - the [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]], the invasion is set to begin on 5 June ([[D-Day (military term)|D-Day]]) with multiple amphibious landings at [[Normandy landings|Normandy, France]]. Aware of invasion's enormity, and equally devastated by the failure of the pre-D-Day rehearsal [[Exercise Tiger]] six weeks earlier, he is privately wary of the operation.

On 2 June, Eisenhower summons [[Met Office]] [[meteorologist]] Gp Capt. [[James Stagg]]{{efn|In truth, Stagg was a geophysicist by training.}} to [[Southwick House]], the seat of the [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force]] (SHAEF) and requests him to provide a forecast favorable for Allied operations for D-Day, which is set to commence in the next 61 hours. Duly appointed as SHAEF's chief meteorological officer{{efn|Stagg joined SHAEF in November 1943, seven months before D-Day.}}, Stagg leads the British-U.S. team tasked with predicting D-Day's forecast, and is introduced to the bombastic Col. [[Irving P. Krick]], who leads the U.S. section of the team. 

Stagg immediately has the team compile and analyze [[meteorological intelligence]] collected by all weather stations within a 2,000 kilometre radius of Normandy to prepare a comprehensive forecast, and promptly predicts two [[Low-pressure area|low-pressure storms]] headed straight for the [[English Channel]] - indicating heavy rain, cloudy skies, low visibility and high waves, which could render the invasion unfeasible. Krick, who has relied more on "analog forecasting" ie., the interpretation of current weather based on historical weather patterns, disputes this, arguing that previous forecasts in the area for the last forty years have indicated nothing inclement. 

On 3 June, Stagg attends the morning conference of SHAEF's top leadership and presents his findings, determining that the planned date of 5 June would be disastrous and recommends the invasion be postponed to 18 June; however, the meeting inconclusively ends when Montgomery mentions any postponement could risk the Allied forces being discovered by the Germans. Krick, who had been barred by Stagg from attending the conference, later meets with Eisenhower and presents his own findings, leading Eisenhower to furiously confront Stagg, who maintains his position. The impasse persists well into the next day without any conclusion; Eisenhower is ambivalent, but nevertheless exhibits a slight inclination towards Krick. Concurrently, Stagg is informed that the hospital where his pregnant wife is convalescing has been bombed, with her condition unknown; although devastated, he does not defer to Krick. Stagg is later comforted by Eisenhower's private secretary and close confidante [[Kay Summersby]], who later asks Eisenhower to not be harsh on him. 

On 4 June, both Stagg and Krick present their respective contradictory findings to SHAEF, which still contradict each other. Exasperated, Stagg points out the anomalies in Krick's forecasting techniques, arguing that the [[Battle of Mont Sorrel]] of June 1925 - which Krick had omitted to mention, also had inclement weather, and that nature cannot be factually ignored; Stagg again insists on postponing to 18 June, but a bullish Montgomery rejects it. However, other SHAEF commanders including Adm. [[Bertram Ramsay]] and ACM. [[Trafford Leigh-Mallory]] hesitate, noting the air and sea components of the invasion cannot work under Stagg's scenario; Eisenhower finally relents on a postponement. Later that morning, SHAEF attends Sunday Mass and despite the initial sunshine, the storms finally arrives, which finally vindicates Stagg but leaves Krick crestfallen.

Despite inclement weather persevering throughout the day, Stagg gets a break when data recorded by one [[Maureen Flavin Sweeney|Maureen Sweeney]] indicates a gap in the stormy weather, which Krick also confirms. In the early hours of 5 June, Stagg briefs Eisenhower and convinces him to launch the invasion on 6 June, which Eisenhower agrees to. In private, Eisenhower and Kay prepare two public statements to be released contingent upon either the invasion's success or failure.

On 6 June, the revised D-Day, Eisenhower delivers a stirring radio addresses to the Allied forces, wishing them victory. Operation Overlord begins with a combined seaborne-cum-airborne thrust on Normandy, which catches the Germans unaware. Elsewhere, celebrations erupt at Southwick House when news of the invasion's success arrives via radio. With his work done, Stagg departs for the hospital where his wife is, and discovers that she and their newborn son had survived, and the three tearfully embrace.

The film's closing [[intertitles]] reveal that the invasion's success emboldened the Allies to defeat Germany within a year, with Eisenhower later mentioning to [[John F. Kennedy|JFK]] in 1961 that Overlord's success was because the Allies "had better meteorologists than the Germans".

== Plot ==
In 1944, at the height of the Second World War, the [[Allies of World War II|Allied powers]] prepare to invade [[German-occupied Europe]] under [[Operation Overlord]]. Helmed by Gen. [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] - the [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]], the invasion is set to begin on 5 June ([[D-Day (military term)|D-Day]]) with multiple amphibious landings at [[Normandy landings|Normandy, France]]. Aware of invasion's enormity, and equally devastated by the failure of the pre-D-Day rehearsal [[Exercise Tiger]] six weeks earlier, he is privately wary of the operation.

On 2 June, Eisenhower summons [[Met Office]] [[meteorologist]] Gp Capt. [[James Stagg]]{{efn|In truth, Stagg was a geophysicist by training.}} to [[Southwick House]], the seat of the [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force]] (SHAEF) and requests him to provide a forecast favorable for Allied operations for D-Day, which is set to commence in the next 61 hours. Duly appointed as SHAEF's chief meteorological officer{{efn|Stagg joined SHAEF in November 1943, seven months before D-Day.}}, Stagg leads the British-U.S. team tasked with predicting D-Day's forecast, and is introduced to the bombastic Col. [[Irving P. Krick]], who leads the U.S. section of the team. 

Stagg immediately has the team compile and analyze [[meteorological intelligence]] collected by all weather stations within a 2,000 kilometre radius of Normandy to prepare a comprehensive forecast, and promptly predicts two [[Low-pressure area|low-pressure storms]] headed straight for the [[English Channel]] - indicating heavy rain, cloudy skies, low visibility and high waves, which could render the invasion unfeasible. Krick, who has relied more on "analog forecasting" ie., the interpretation of current weather based on historical weather patterns, disputes this, arguing that previous forecasts in the area for the last forty years have indicated nothing inclement. 

On 3 June, Stagg attends the morning conference of SHAEF's top leadership and presents his findings, determining that the planned date of 5 June would be disastrous and recommends the invasion be postponed to 18 June, which earns the ire of General [[Bernard Montgomery]], who insists on continuing nonetheless; the meeting ends without a conclusion. Krick, who had been barred by Stagg from attending the conference, meets with Eisenhower the same night and presents his own findings, leading Eisenhower to furiously confront Stagg, who maintains his position. The impasse persists well into the next day, with Stagg accusing Krick's forecast of being "moronic"; Eisenhower is ambivalent, but nevertheless exhibits a slight inclination towards Krick. Concurrently, Stagg is informed that the hospital where his pregnant wife is convalescing has been bombed, with her condition unknown; although devastated, he does not defer to Krick. Stagg is later comforted by Eisenhower's private secretary and close confidante [[Kay Summersby]], who later asks Eisenhower to not be harsh on him. 

On 4 June, both Stagg and Krick present their respective contradictory findings to SHAEF, which still contradict each other. Exasperated, Stagg points out the anomalies in Krick's forecasting techniques, arguing that the [[Battle of Mont Sorrel]] of June 1925 - which Krick had omitted to mention, also had inclement weather, and that nature cannot be factually ignored; Stagg again insists on postponing to 18 June, but a bullish Montgomery rejects it. However, other SHAEF commanders including Adm. [[Bertram Ramsay]] and ACM. [[Trafford Leigh-Mallory]] hesitate, noting the air and sea components of the invasion cannot work under Stagg's condition; Eisenhower finally relents on a postponement. Later that morning, SHAEF attends Sunday Mass and despite the initial sunshine, the storms finally arrives, which finally vindicates Stagg but leaves Krick crestfallen.

Despite inclement weather persevering throughout the day, Stagg gets a break when data recorded by one [[Maureen Flavin Sweeney|Maureen Sweeney]] indicates a gap in the stormy weather, which Krick also confirms. In the early hours of 5 June, Stagg brief Eisenhower on the developments and convinces him to launch the invasion on 6 June, which Eisenhower agrees to. In private, Eisenhower and Kay prepare two public statements to be released contingent upon either the invasion's success or failure.
